claims.source: To evaluate the sensitivity of the method, we varied the amount of immunoprecipitates from 40 μg to 3 μg of proteins and found that the number of inter-link identifications did not change much as the input decreased from 40 to 20 μg (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: The results section presents data on the sensitivity of the method.

claims.claim: From three experiments starting with 40 μg of proteins from the Rrp46 immunoprecipitate, a total of 195 cross-linked lysine pairs (43 inter-molecular and 152 intra-molecular) were identified.
claims.source: From three experiments starting with 40 μg of proteins, a total of 195 cross-linked lysine pairs (43 inter-molecular and 152 intra-molecular) were identified (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 4).
claims.evidence: The results section provides specific numbers of cross-links identified from the exosome immunoprecipitate.

claims.claim: Cross-linking helped identify all ten exosome core subunits and 15 putative direct protein-protein interactions amongst the core subunits.
claims.source: Thanks to cross-linking, not only did we identify all ten exosome core subunits, but also 15 putative direct protein-protein interactions amongst the core subunits, which generated a connectivity map more complete than the one from yeast two-hybrid experiments (Stark et al., 2006; Uetz et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2002; Luz et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2008) and showed that among the co-immunoprecipitated proteins, Rrp41 and Rrp45 directly bind to the bait protein Rrp46 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The results section states the number of exosome subunits and interactions identified.

claims.claim: The connectivity map generated from Leiker cross-links is more complete than the one from yeast two-hybrid experiments.
claims.source: Thanks to cross-linking, not only did we identify all ten exosome core subunits, but also 15 putative direct protein-protein interactions amongst the core subunits, which generated a connectivity map more complete than the one from yeast two-hybrid experiments (Stark et al., 2006; Uetz et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2002; Luz et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2008) and showed that among the co-immunoprecipitated proteins, Rrp41 and Rrp45 directly bind to the bait protein Rrp46 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The results section compares the connectivity map to yeast two-hybrid data.

claims.claim: Rrp41 and Rrp45 directly bind to the bait protein Rrp46.
claims.source: Thanks to cross-linking, not only did we identify all ten exosome core subunits, but also 15 putative direct protein-protein interactions amongst the core subunits, which generated a connectivity map more complete than the one from yeast two-hybrid experiments (Stark et al., 2006; Uetz et al., 2000; Oliveira et al., 2002; Luz et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2008) and showed that among the co-immunoprecipitated proteins, Rrp41 and Rrp45 directly bind to the bait protein Rrp46 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The results section identifies Rrp41 and Rrp45 as direct binding partners of Rrp46.

claims.claim: 69% of the cross-links identified from the exosome immunoprecipitate were compatible with the crystal structure of an RNA-bound 11-subunit exosome complex.
claims.source: Of the cross-links identified, 69% were compatible with the crystal structure of an RNA-bound 11-subunit exosome complex (Makino et al., 2013) (PDB code: 4IFD).
claims.evidence: The results section provides structural validation data for exosome cross-links.

claims.claim: Among the cross-links that disagreed with the RNA-bound exosome structure, 68% involved the catalytic subunit Rrp44.
claims.source: Among the cross-links that disagreed with the RNA-bound structure, 68% involved the catalytic subunit Rrp44, which has a large rotation relative to the rest of the exosome core between the RNA-bound and the RNA-free states (Makino et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The results section analyzes the incompatible cross-links and relates them to Rrp44's conformational changes.

claims.claim: The presence or absence of bound RNA is likely to be the primary reason behind most of the seemingly inconsistent inter-molecular cross-links in the exosome.
claims.source: The crude Rrp46 immunoprecipitate should mainly contain apo exosome, because magnesium was included in the buffer to activate the nuclease activity of exosome. Therefore, the presence (in the crystal structure) or absence (in our exosome preparation) of bound RNA is likely to be the primary reason behind most of the seemingly inconsistent inter-molecular cross-links.
claims.evidence: The results section proposes this explanation for the incompatible cross-links based on the sample preparation.

claims.claim: Two known (Mpp6 and Ski7) and four potential exosome regulators were found through nine cross-links with core exosome subunits.
claims.source: To fulfill different functions in multiple biological processes (Houseley and Tollervey, 2009), the core exosome complex must recruit additional regulators, of which only a few are known. Here we found two known (Mpp6 [Milligan et al., 2008] and Ski7 Araki et al., 2001) and four potential exosome regulators through nine cross-links with core exosome subunits (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 4).
claims.evidence: The results section identifies known and potential exosome regulators based on cross-link data.

claims.claim: Ski7 was found to cross-link with Rrp4 via K111.
claims.source: Ski7 was found to cross-link with Rrp4 via K111, which fits well with previous co-IP results obtained by using different fragments of Ski7 (Araki et al., 2001) and a recently published CXMS study of the yeast exosome (Shi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The results section provides specific cross-link data for Ski7 and validates it against previous studies.

claims.claim: The translation initiation factor Tif1 had interactions with the Rrp4 and Rrp44 exosome subunits.
claims.source: Among the newly identified candidate regulators, the translation initiation factor Tif1 stood out; it had interactions with the Rrp4 and Rrp44 exosome subunits (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The results section identifies Tif1 as a candidate exosome regulator based on cross-link data.

claims.claim: Translation has been implicated in RNA quality control.
claims.source: Translation has been implicated in RNA quality control (Shoemaker and Green, 2012).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a study linking translation to RNA quality control.

claims.claim: The linkages between Tif1 and exosome subunits support the hypothesis that exosome complexes 'stand by' the translation machinery and recognize and degrade aberrant mRNA molecules.
claims.source: The linkages identified here support the hypothesis that exosome complexes 'stand by' the translation machinery and recognize and degrade aberrant mRNA molecules.
claims.evidence: The results section proposes this hypothesis based on the Tif1-exosome cross-links.

claims.claim: In three independent experiments with E. coli whole-cell lysates, a total of 2003 non-redundant inter-linked lysine pairs were identified including 1386 (69%) intra-molecular and 617 (32%) inter-molecular cross-links.
claims.source: In three independent experiments, Leiker-treated, trypsin digested E. coli lysates were fractionated on a high pH reverse phase column, and cross-linked peptides were enriched from each of the 10 or 11 fractions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). After filtering the data by requiring FDR < 0.05, E-value < 0.01, spectral count ≥ 3, we identified a total of 2003 non-redundant inter-linked lysine pairs including 1386 (69%) intra-molecular and 617 (32%) inter-molecular cross-links (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The results section provides specific numbers of cross-links identified from E. coli lysates.

claims.claim: Protein structure information is available in the PDB database for 984 intra-molecular cross-links from E. coli lysates, and is consistent with 80% of them.
claims.source: Protein structure information is available in the PDB database for 984 intra-molecular cross-links identified with Leiker, and is consistent with 80% of them, indicating the high quality of the results (Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The results section provides structural validation data for E. coli cross-links.

claims.claim: The inter-molecular cross-links from E. coli lysates represent 436 pairs of protein-protein interactions.
claims.source: Of note, the inter-molecular cross-links represent 436 pairs of protein-protein interactions, and 25% of the cross-links are supported by the combined network of the bacteriome.org database (Peregrín-Alvarez et al., 2009) Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The results section states the number of PPIs represented by the cross-links.

claims.claim: 25% of the inter-molecular cross-links from E. coli lysates are supported by the combined network of the bacteriome.org database.
claims.source: Of note, the inter-molecular cross-links represent 436 pairs of protein-protein interactions, and 25% of the cross-links are supported by the combined network of the bacteriome.org database (Peregrín-Alvarez et al., 2009) Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The results section validates a portion of the cross-links against an existing database.

claims.claim: Most of the inter-molecular cross-links from E. coli lysates suggest novel protein-protein interactions.
claims.source: Of note, the inter-molecular cross-links represent 436 pairs of protein-protein interactions, and 25% of the cross-links are supported by the combined network of the bacteriome.org database (Peregrín-Alvarez et al., 2009) Figure 5—source data 1). Most of the inter-molecular cross-links suggest novel protein-protein interactions.
claims.evidence: The results section states this explicitly, and it follows logically from the fact that only 25% are supported by existing databases.

claims.claim: The most highly connected module extracted from the E. coli protein-protein interaction network consists of 9 ribosomal proteins and two DNA-binding proteins (the Hu heterodimer DBHA/DBHB) organized around a translation elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu).
claims.source: Based on the Leiker cross-links, we constructed a protein-protein interaction network and extracted the most highly connected module (Bader and Hogue, 2003; Saito et al., 2012) (Figure 5A). This 12-protein module consists of 9 ribosomal proteins and two DNA-binding proteins (the Hu heterodimer DBHA/DBHB) organized around a translation elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the composition of the most connected module.

claims.claim: The most highly connected module from E. coli is enriched with proteins that function in translation.
claims.source: Evidently, it is enriched with proteins that function in translation, suggesting that DBHA/DBHB also plays a role in this process.
claims.evidence: The results section characterizes the functional enrichment of the module.

claims.claim: DBHA/DBHB plays a role in translation.
claims.source: Evidently, it is enriched with proteins that function in translation, suggesting that DBHA/DBHB also plays a role in this process.
claims.evidence: The results section proposes this based on the network analysis.

claims.claim: A small fraction of the Hu heterodimer is bound to ribosomes.
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies reported that a small fraction of this Hu heterodimer is bound to ribosomes (Rouvière-Yaniv and Kjeldgaard, 1979) and that this protein can enhance or repress translation of the mRNA molecules that it binds to (Balandina et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The results section cites previous studies showing Hu heterodimer binding to ribosomes.

claims.claim: The Hu heterodimer can enhance or repress translation of the mRNA molecules that it binds to.
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies reported that a small fraction of this Hu heterodimer is bound to ribosomes (Rouvière-Yaniv and Kjeldgaard, 1979) and that this protein can enhance or repress translation of the mRNA molecules that it binds to (Balandina et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a previous study showing the Hu heterodimer's role in translation regulation.

claims.claim: The most connected module obtained from previously identified BS3 cross-links comprised only three ribosomal proteins.
claims.source: In contrast, the most connected module obtained from the previously identified BS3 cross-links (Yang et al., 2012) comprised only three ribosomal proteins (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The results section compares the Leiker results to previous BS3 results.

claims.claim: Leiker has potential in generating comprehensive protein-protein interaction networks using CXMS.
claims.source: These results indicate the potential of Leiker in generating comprehensive protein-protein interaction networks using CXMS.
claims.evidence: The results section draws this conclusion based on the E. coli network analysis.

claims.claim: Analysis of ribo-free E. coli samples with Leiker identified 1971 inter-links, 1127 of which were not identified in the whole-cell lysates.
claims.source: Since ribosomal proteins dominated E. coli whole-cell lysates, we prepared samples in which ribosomes were removed by centrifugation through a layer of sucrose cushion. Analysis of the ribo-free samples (two repeats) with Leiker identified 1971 inter-links, 1127 of which were not identified in the whole-cell lysates (5% FDR, E-value < 0.01, spectral count ≥ 3) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Figure 5—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The results section provides specific numbers of cross-links identified from ribo-free samples.

claims.claim: Together, a total of 3130 non-redundant cross-linked lysine pairs were identified from E. coli, allowing construction of a network comprising 677 protein-protein interactions.
claims.source: Together, we identified a total of 3130 non-redundant cross-linked lysine pairs from E. coli. This allowed us to construct a network comprising 677 protein-protein interactions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The results section provides the total number of cross-links and PPIs from combined E. coli samples.

claims.claim: From C. elegans whole-worm lysate, 459 inter-links were identified (5% FDR, E-value < 0.01, spectral count ≥ 3).
claims.source: Applying Leiker to an even more complex lysate from C. elegans, which has a similar number of protein coding genes as human (~20,000), we identified 459 inter-links (5% FDR, E-value < 0.01, spectral count ≥ 3) (Figure 5—source data 3).
claims.evidence: The results section provides specific numbers of cross-links identified from C. elegans lysate.

claims.claim: From C. elegans mitochondrial fraction, 547 inter-linked lysine pairs were identified, of which 434 were not detected in the whole-worm lysate.

claims.evidence: The results section provides specific numbers of cross-links identified from C. elegans mitochondria.

claims.claim: Together, 893 non-redundant cross-linked lysine pairs were identified from C. elegans, constructing protein-protein interactions between 155 proteins.
claims.source: Together, we identified 893 non-redundant cross-linked lysine pairs from C. elegans and constructed protein-protein interactions between 155 proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The results section provides the total number of cross-links and proteins from combined C. elegans samples.

claims.claim: The number of C. elegans cross-links identified in this study was 23 times as many as the previous record.

claims.evidence: The results section compares the current C. elegans results to a previous study.

claims.claim: The number of E. coli cross-links identified in this study is four times greater than the number of PIR-identified inter-links.

claims.evidence: The results section compares the current E. coli results to previous studies using different cross-linkers.

claims.claim: The number of E. coli cross-links identified in this study is eight times greater than the number of BS3-identified inter-links.
claims.source: The number of E. coli cross-links identified in this study is four times greater than the number of PIR-identified inter-links (Chavez et al., 2013) and eight times greater than the number of BS3-identified inter-links (Yang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The results section compares the current E. coli results to previous studies using different cross-linkers.

claims.claim: Half of the BS3-identified cross-links were recapitulated in this study.
claims.source: Half of the BS3-identified cross-links (Yang et al., 2012) were recapitulated in this study (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The results section compares the overlap between Leiker and BS3 cross-links.

claims.claim: Mono-links at all 15 lysine residues and the N-terminus of L7Ae were reliably quantified in both forward and reverse labeling experiments.
claims.source: Mono-linked peptides are usually neglected in CXMS, but they are valuable because they indicate that the modified lysine residues are exposed to solvent. Mono-links at all 15 lysine residues and the N-terminus of L7Ae were reliably quantified (Figure 6) in both forward and reverse labeling experiments.
claims.evidence: The results section states that all L7Ae mono-links were quantified.

claims.claim: Three mono-links at K35, K42, and K84 of L7Ae consistently had significantly higher abundance (>5 fold) in the RNA-free state than in the RNA-bound state.
claims.source: Three mono-links at K35, K42, and K84 consistently had significantly higher abundance (>5 fold) in the RNA-free state (F) than in the RNA-bound state (B) (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The results section provides specific quantification data for L7Ae mono-links.

claims.claim: The three lysine residues K35, K42, and K84 of L7Ae are buried upon RNA binding.
claims.source: These results suggest that the three lysine residues are buried upon RNA binding, either due to direct protein-RNA binding or indirect protein conformational changes induced by RNA binding. This is in perfect agreement with the crystal structure (Li and Ye, 2006) (PDB code: 2HVY), which shows that K35, K42, and K84 all bind to the RNA, each with a buried area greater than 20 Å2 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The results section validates the quantitative CXMS findings against the crystal structure.

claims.claim: K35, K42, and K84 of L7Ae all bind to the RNA, each with a buried area greater than 20 Å2.
claims.source: This is in perfect agreement with the crystal structure (Li and Ye, 2006) (PDB code: 2HVY), which shows that K35, K42, and K84 all bind to the RNA, each with a buried area greater than 20 Å2 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The results section cites the crystal structure showing RNA binding and buried surface areas.

claims.claim: A total of 161 inter-linked lysine pairs from E. coli lysates were quantified in both the forward and the reverse labeling experiments comparing log phase and stationary phase.
claims.source: Lastly, we applied quantitative CXMS to E. coli lysates. The log phase and the stationary phase cell lysates were cross-linked, respectively, with [d0]- and [d6]-bAL2 in the forward labeling experiment, or with [d6]- and [d0]-bAL2 in the reverse labeling experiment. After a single enrichment step without pre-fractionation, a total of 161 inter-linked lysine pairs were quantified in both the forward and the reverse labeling experiments, and most of them had similar [log phase]/[stationary phase] ratios in the two experiments (Figure 8 and Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The results section provides the number of quantified cross-links from E. coli growth phase comparison.

claims.claim: The cross-link between YqjD and ElaB increased at least 10 times in the stationary phase compared to the log phase.
claims.source: Noticeably, the cross-link between YqjD and ElaB increased at least 10 times in the stationary phase compared to the log phase.

claims.claim: YqjD and ElaB are paralogous proteins associated with the inner membrane of E. coli cells through their C-terminal transmembrane motifs.
claims.source: These two paralogous proteins are associated with the inner membrane of E. coli cells through their C-terminal transmembrane motifs and both bind to stationary phase ribosomes, probably through their N-terminal regions (Yoshida et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a study characterizing YqjD and ElaB.

claims.claim: YqjD and ElaB both bind to stationary phase ribosomes, probably through their N-terminal regions.
claims.source: These two paralogous proteins are associated with the inner membrane of E. coli cells through their C-terminal transmembrane motifs and both bind to stationary phase ribosomes, probably through their N-terminal regions (Yoshida et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a study showing YqjD and ElaB binding to ribosomes.

claims.claim: YqjD binding to ribosomes inhibits translation.
claims.source: It is suggested that YqjD binding to ribosomes inhibits translation (Yoshida et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a study suggesting YqjD's role in translation inhibition.

claims.claim: Association of YqjD and ElaB has been detected but the sites of interaction are not known.
claims.source: Association of YqjD and ElaB has been detected but the sites of interaction are not known (Hu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a study showing YqjD-ElaB association without site information.

claims.claim: YqjD and ElaB form a heterodimer through their central regions, presumably as a stronger, divalent anchoring site for ribosomes to inhibit protein translation in the stationary phase.
claims.source: Here, our results not only confirm previous findings, but also provide new insights that YqjD and ElaB form a heterodimer through their central regions, presumably as a stronger, divalent anchoring site for ribosomes to inhibit protein translation in the stationary phase.
claims.evidence: The results section proposes this model based on the quantitative CXMS data.

claims.claim: Leiker yields a fourfold increase in the number of identified cross-linked peptide pairs from complex samples with an enrichment efficiency of 97% or more.
claims.source: In this study, we developed an MS-friendly and isotope-encodable cross-linker called Leiker that enables the efficient enrichment of cross-linked peptides through biotin-based immobilization and azobenzene-based chemical cleavage. With an enrichment efficiency of 97% or more, Leiker yields a fourfold increase in the number of identified cross-linked peptide pairs from complex samples.
claims.evidence: The discussion summarizes the key findings about Leiker's performance.

claims.claim: A workflow for quantitative CXMS based on deuterium-labeled Leiker was established.
claims.source: Also established is a workflow for quantitative CXMS based on deuterium-labeled Leiker.
claims.evidence: The discussion states this as an established method.

claims.claim: A comprehensive network of putative direct protein-protein interactions could be obtained by applying Leiker to lysates.
claims.source: In theory, a comprehensive network of putative direct protein-protein interactions could be obtained by applying Leiker to lysates.
claims.evidence: The discussion presents this as a theoretical possibility.

claims.claim: The interaction networks obtained from lysates are limited because the cross-links identified are dominated by those from highly abundant proteins.

claims.evidence: The discussion identifies this as a limitation of the lysate approach.

claims.claim: Subcellular fractionation can overcome the limitation of abundant proteins dominating cross-link identifications.

claims.evidence: The discussion proposes subcellular fractionation as a solution to the limitation.

claims.claim: The number of unique inter-link identifications increased by more than 50% (from 2003 to 3130) by removing ribosomes from E. coli lysates.

claims.evidence: The discussion quantifies the improvement from ribosome removal.

claims.claim: Extensive protein fractionation coupled with Leiker-assisted CXMS will pave the way towards constructing comprehensive interactomes for different model organisms.
claims.source: We anticipate that extensive protein fractionation coupled with Leiker-assisted CXMS will pave the way towards constructing comprehensive interactomes for different model organisms, and next-generation cross-link identification software of higher sensitivity will also help.
claims.evidence: The discussion presents this as an anticipated future application.

claims.claim: Leiker shows promise for use in differential interactome analysis.
claims.source: Further, with the advantage of heavy isotope labeling for quantification in addition to the enrichment function, Leiker shows promise for use in differential interactome analysis (Ideker and Krogan, 2012).
claims.evidence: The discussion presents this as a promising application based on Leiker's capabilities.

claims.claim: The intra-molecular cross-links in both E. coli whole-cell lysates and ribo-free samples had similar rates of structural compatibility (80% and 84%, respectively).
claims.source: When we examined the cross-links identified from E. coli against the protein structures deposited in the PDB database, we noted that the intra-molecular cross-links in both the whole-cell lysates and the ribo-free samples had similar rates of structural compatibility (80% and 84%, respectively). This shows that the quality of our Leiker-based CXMS data is high.
claims.evidence: The discussion compares structural compatibility rates to assess data quality.

claims.claim: The inter-molecular cross-links detected from the ribo-free samples had a much higher rate of structural compatibility (69%) than those detected in the whole-cell lysates (12%).
claims.source: Interestingly, the inter-molecular cross-links detected from the ribo-free samples had a much higher rate of structural compatibility (69%) than those detected in the whole-cell lysates (12%).
claims.evidence: The discussion compares structural compatibility rates between sample types.

claims.claim: Most of the apparently incompatible inter-molecular cross-links seen in the whole-cell lysates likely result from cross-linking of adjacent ribosomal particles.
claims.source: Given that 92% of the inter-links with existing structural information in the whole-cell lysate involved at least one ribosomal protein and many were between ribosomal proteins, we think that most of the apparently incompatible inter-molecular cross-links seen in the whole-cell lysates likely result from cross-linking of adjacent ribosomal particles.
claims.evidence: The discussion proposes this explanation for the low structural compatibility in whole-cell lysates.

claims.claim: Previous cross-linking studies have typically treated mono-linked peptides as by-products and ignored them.
claims.source: Previous cross-linking studies have typically treated mono-linked peptides as by-products, and have ignored them.
claims.evidence: The discussion characterizes the historical treatment of mono-links in CXMS.

results.result: The authors developed Leiker, a trifunctional cross-linker with a biotin tag, azobenzene-based cleavage site, and isotope-encodable spacer arm. After testing multiple designs, bAL1 and bAL2 performed best with equivalent performance, featuring a 9.3-Å spacer arm shorter than BS3 and producing a characteristic reporter ion at m/z 122.0606.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C17-C23 collectively describe the design, synthesis, and characterization of Leiker with consistent experimental evidence. The structural features are explicitly stated (C18), the performance comparison is documented (C17), and the reporter ion is demonstrated (C20). The isotope labeling with six deuterium atoms (C22-C23) is validated experimentally.

results.result: Leiker enables highly efficient enrichment of cross-linked peptides with >97% enrichment efficiency and maintains specificity comparable to BS3. In E. coli lysates, Leiker yielded at least a fourfold increase in inter-link identifications compared to BS3, with 82% of cross-links having Cα-Cα distances ≤22 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are strongly supported by direct experimental comparisons shown in Figure 3. The >97% enrichment efficiency (C24) is demonstrated across dilution series, structural validation confirms distance constraints (C25-C26), and specificity is equivalent to BS3 at 3% artifactual cross-links (C27). The fourfold improvement (C28) is directly measured.

results.result: Application of Leiker to purified E. coli 70S ribosome identified 222 inter-linked lysine pairs (95 inter-molecular, 127 intra-molecular), three times more than a previous study. Structural validation showed 75% of cross-links compatible with crystal structure at ≤22 Å, with higher compatibility for intra-molecular (84%) than inter-molecular (50% at ≤22 Å, 73% at ≤30 Å) cross-links.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 present consistent quantitative data on ribosome cross-linking with appropriate structural validation against PDB 5AFI. The threefold improvement over previous work (C30) provides context, and the distance distribution analysis (C31-C34) appropriately accounts for conformational flexibility. The lower inter-molecular compatibility is reasonably attributed to protein dynamics.

results.result: Cross-linking data revealed conformational flexibility of ribosomal protein L9, including evidence of bending consistent with cryo-EM structures and long-distance cross-links (>50 Å) interpreted as inter-ribosomal particle interactions. Negative staining EM confirmed ribosome oligomerization in the absence of mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C41 provide converging evidence for L9 flexibility from multiple sources: b-factors (C35), published structures (C36), cross-link patterns (C37-C38), and EM validation (C41). The interpretation of long-distance cross-links as inter-particle interactions (C39) is reasonable given L9's location at particle interfaces (C40) and is supported by independent EM evidence.

results.result: Leiker-based CXMS provided structural information on flexible peripheral ribosomal proteins (S1, L1, L7/12, L31) that are refractory to crystallography and cryo-EM. Novel findings include extensive S1-L1 contacts suggesting coordination between tRNA release and mRNA exit, S1-S2 N-terminal interactions, L1 rotated conformation, L7/12 contacts with the 30S subunit, and L31 localization to the central protuberance.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C42-C61 collectively demonstrate Leiker's utility for studying dynamic ribosomal regions. The identification of peripheral proteins with most cross-links (C44-C45) is data-driven, and specific findings are validated against existing structures where available (C55, C57, C60). Novel interactions (C50-C52, C58-C59) are appropriately presented as new discoveries with mechanistic hypotheses that require further validation.

results.result: From a crude Rrp46 immunoprecipitate containing 740 proteins, Leiker identified 195 cross-linked lysine pairs including all ten exosome core subunits, 15 core subunit interactions, and two direct Rrp46 binding partners (Rrp41, Rrp45). The method also identified known regulators (Mpp6, Ski7) and candidate regulators including Tif1, suggesting exosome-translation machinery coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C62-C75 demonstrate Leiker's effectiveness in complex immunoprecipitates. The connectivity map is more complete than yeast two-hybrid data (C66), and 69% of cross-links are compatible with the RNA-bound exosome structure (C68). The identification of Tif1 as a candidate regulator (C73-C75) is appropriately presented as hypothesis-generating, supported by the translation-RNA quality control link (C74).

results.result: Application of Leiker to E. coli lysates identified 3130 inter-linked lysine pairs representing 677 PPIs, with 80% of intra-molecular cross-links structurally validated. The most connected network module comprised 12 proteins including 9 ribosomal proteins and the Hu heterodimer (DBHA/DBHB) organized around EF-Tu, suggesting DBHA/DBHB involvement in translation. Ribosome removal increased identifications by 50%.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C76-C89 present comprehensive lysate analysis with appropriate quality metrics (80% structural compatibility, C77). The network analysis identifying DBHA/DBHB in a translation-enriched module (C81-C83) is supported by prior literature (C84-C85). The improvement from ribosome depletion (C88, C113) demonstrates a practical solution to the abundant protein problem (C111).

results.result: Application of Leiker to C. elegans lysates identified 893 inter-linked lysine pairs representing 121 PPIs, 23 times more than previous records. Analysis of whole-worm and mitochondrial fractions showed substantial non-overlap (434 of 547 mitochondrial cross-links were unique), demonstrating the value of subcellular fractionation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C90-C96 demonstrate Leiker's effectiveness in a eukaryotic system with appropriate comparisons to prior work (C93-C95). The substantial improvement over previous methods is clearly documented, and the complementarity of whole-cell and fractionated samples (C91) supports the fractionation strategy discussed in C112-C113.

results.result: Quantitative CXMS using deuterium-labeled Leiker successfully mapped RNA-binding lysine residues in L7Ae. Three lysine residues (K35, K42, K84) showed >5-fold higher mono-link abundance in the RNA-free state, perfectly agreeing with the crystal structure showing these residues bind RNA with >20 Å² buried surface area each.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C97-C100, C109, C121 demonstrate successful quantitative CXMS with strong validation. All 15 lysine residues were quantified (C97), three showed significant changes (C98), and the results perfectly match the crystal structure (C99-C100). This proof-of-principle experiment validates both the quantitative workflow (C109) and the utility of mono-links (C121).

results.result: Quantitative CXMS of E. coli log phase versus stationary phase lysates identified 161 quantified inter-linked lysine pairs. The YqjD-ElaB cross-link increased >10-fold in stationary phase, revealing that these paralogous proteins form a heterodimer through their central regions, likely serving as a divalent ribosome anchoring site for translation inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C107 present quantitative analysis of a complex biological system with a striking finding (>10-fold change, C102). The interpretation is supported by prior knowledge of YqjD/ElaB properties (C103-C106) and extends previous findings by identifying the interaction site (C107). The model is reasonable but appropriately presented as a hypothesis requiring further validation.

results.result: Leiker yields a fourfold increase in cross-link identifications with 97% enrichment efficiency, enabling comprehensive protein-protein interaction network mapping. However, networks from lysates are limited by abundant proteins dominating identifications, which can be overcome by subcellular fractionation (demonstrated by 50% increase after ribosome removal). The method shows promise for differential interactome analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C108, C110-C115 provide an accurate summary of Leiker's capabilities and limitations. The performance metrics (C108) are well-documented, the limitation from abundant proteins (C111) is clearly demonstrated, and the solution via fractionation (C112-C113) is validated experimentally. Future applications (C114-C115) are appropriately presented as anticipated rather than demonstrated.

results.result: Intra-molecular cross-links from E. coli lysates showed consistently high structural compatibility (80-84%) in both whole-cell and ribo-free samples. However, inter-molecular cross-links showed much higher compatibility in ribo-free samples (69%) versus whole-cell lysates (12%), likely because whole-cell lysate cross-links predominantly involve ribosomal proteins and reflect inter-ribosomal particle interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 present a thoughtful analysis of data quality with a reasonable explanation for the observed differences. The high intra-molecular compatibility validates data quality (C116), and the interpretation that low inter-molecular compatibility in whole-cell lysates reflects inter-particle cross-linking (C118) is consistent with the L9 findings (C38-C41) and the observation that 92% of incompatible inter-links involve ribosomal proteins.

results.result: Mono-linked peptides, typically ignored in CXMS studies, carry structural information and outnumber inter-links. This study demonstrates their value for mapping RNA-binding lysine residues and proposes that quantitative mono-link analysis is particularly suited for mapping DNA/RNA binding surfaces due to lysine's frequent involvement in binding negatively charged nucleic acid backbones.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C124 make a compelling case for utilizing mono-link data. The historical neglect (C119) is accurately characterized, the abundance and information content (C120) are demonstrated in Figure 3, the utility for RNA binding is proven with L7Ae (C121), and the proposed application (C123) is logically grounded in lysine's chemical properties (C122). The recommendation (C124) is well-justified.

results.result: CXMS has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing protein structures and interactions, being less time-consuming and demanding than traditional methods. However, it remains limited by sample complexity and low cross-link abundance, requiring extensive fractionation for complex samples. Despite efforts to develop enrichable cross-linkers, few have improved identification in complex samples, with Azide-A-DSBSO and PIR as exceptions requiring special instrument control.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C16 accurately characterize the state of the CXMS field based on extensive citations. The emergence of CXMS (C7-C9), its limitations (C10-C12), and the gap in enrichable cross-linkers (C13-C16) are well-documented in the literature and provide appropriate context for the development of Leiker.
